title: Non-Equi and Range Joins
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of non-equi and range joins.

content.intro: Learn non-equi and range joins through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Non-Equi and Range Joins matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: The practical goal of non-equi and range joins is to produce a result set whose meaning is clear. Confirm which rows enter the query, how values are transformed or combined, and whether NULLs, duplicates, ties, or one-to-many relationships change the output.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Inequality join conditions, Range-based matching, Date-interval joins, Matching prices, thresholds, and bands. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Inequality join conditions
items.text: Inequality join conditions determines how rows from related sources are matched. Write the join predicate explicitly and check whether multiple matches can multiply rows; use a LEFT JOIN when unmatched left-side records must remain visible.

items.title: Range-based matching
items.text: Range-based matching helps you combine related tables correctly, predict matched and unmatched rows, and diagnose incorrect row multiplication or missing relationships. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Performance considerations
items.text: Performance considerations should be evaluated with measurements on representative data. Inspect the plan, estimated versus actual row counts where available, and the workload's read/write balance; an index or rewrite is not automatically faster.

content_blocks.code:
SELECT o.order_id, c.full_name, o.order_date, o.total_amount
FROM orders AS o
JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
ORDER BY o.order_date DESC, o.order_id DESC;
content_blocks.expected_output: Each order is paired with its customer through the foreign-key relationship. The unique tie-breaker makes the requested order deterministic.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
